Hi, it's Cathy again.  I'm going to help guide you through the first Excel spreadsheet of the first assignment.
I'm McGraph.  I'll help Cathy guide you.  Remember to click on the upper arrow above Cathy in order to advance the "step number."
You will notice that the data for the problem is already on the spreadsheet.
It's almost always a good idea to put the data in the spreadsheet in an easily accesible manner.
There are three decision variables.  Use cells F17:H17 to hold the decision variables.  Now select "Solver" in the menu.

In Office 2008 for the Mac, you will need to open the program "Excel Solver" which is a separate program.  In Office 2011 for the Mac, you need to add Solver via Add-ins.  Then Solver will appear in the tools menu.
Now that you see the Solver window, select "By Changing Cells" and enter "F17:H17".  Alternatively, you could have selected cells F17:H17, and the cell range would be entered into the Solver window.
In Office 2008 for the Mac, you will need to click on the small button in the Solver window containing red and blue dots that is to the left of the word "guess".
You will notice the formatting on this page.  The formating is to help provide some guidance, and is not needed for solving the problem.
You will also notice that we have used the following convention. The decision variables are below the data. Then comes the objective function. Then comes the constraints.
Now close the Solver window by clicking on "close" (in the window).  Then put values 1, 2 and 3 in F17:H17.   These values are just place holders for now.
It's now time to enter the constraints of the problem.
We'll give you some guidance for the first constraint.  Then you can do the remaining constraints on your own.
There are five days of production. This should be put in cell H22. But don't write "5" in cell H22. Instead, write "=I11".

In general, don't write values for the right hand sides of constraints.  Instead, reference the original data.  That way, if the original data is changed, the values in the constraints are automatically changed.
Now express the total manufacturing capacity in terms of the decision variables, and put it in cell F22.   Hopefully, you have already figured out the coefficients.
Make sure that your calculation of the production is correct. For example, if the number of iPhone covers is 10,000, then it accounts for 2 days of production.
Finally, put "<=" in Cell G22.  The purpose of this is to make the spreadsheet easier to read.  It has no impact on any of the computations.
In general, it is a good idea to use "<=", ">=" and "=" when expressing constraints on the spreadsheet, for ease of reading.
Now, select Solver again. To the right o "Subject to the constraints" click on "Add". The cell reference is where the formula for the constraints is held. In this case, it is in cell F22.
The type of the constraint is "<=". The "Constraint" referes to the cell holding the RHS of the constraint. In this case, it is cell H22. After entering "H22", click on "OK".
We have now added the first constraint to the problem.  We could have added it in many different ways.  For example, you could have listed I11 as the "constraint".
But this makes the spreadsheet much harder to read. More importantly, it makes the spreadsheet very hard to debug.
Now add the remaining constraints for storage, the min production of iPod and iPad covers, and the max production of iPod, iPhone, and iPad covers.
Remember that the RHS should reference data in the spreadsheet rather than be entered as a number.
Now it is time to enter the revenue function. Enter the formula for the revenue function.
You should enter the formula in cell F19.
The obvious thing to do is to enter "=4000*F17+6000*G17+10000*H17".
It is both obvious and correct. It is also probably the fastest way of entering the formula.
But we are going to ask you to enter it in a different way. The formula should be "=SUMPRODUCT(F15:H15,F17:H17)".
"F15:H15" is the array in which the data on profit is stored. "F17:H17" is the array holding the decision variables.
SUMPRODUCT creates the inner product of two arrays. In this case, it is equivalent to the formula "F15*F17+G15*G17+H15*H17".
Using SUMPRODUCT requires more effor when there are a few decision variables. But it is much easier when there are lots of decision variables.
For some linear programs, one can create the formula for the first constraint using SUMPRODUCT, and then create the formula for the remaining constraints using a copy-down command.
But if you use this approach, you need to remmebre to use "$F17:$H17" in the first SUMPRODUCT. This would ensure that the other formula using SUMPRODUCT would also contain "$F17:$H17".
Figuring out when to use "$" in fomrula takes some practice.  But once it is learned, it is extremely useful.
Now open up Solver again, and put "F19" into "Set target Cell".
We are almost ready to click on "Solve."  But first, you need to click on "Max" which is to the right of "Equal To."  (If it was already selected, you don't need to do anything).
If you had clicked on "Min", Solver would have determined the solution with the minimum revenue.
You still need to say that all variables are nonnegative and  that the problem is a linear program.  This can occur either on the dialogue box in front of you or by clicking on options.

Different versions of Excel have different ways of doing this.  In Excel 2010 and 2011 this is done on the first dialogue box.  To say that it is an LP, write that Simplex should be used as the solution method.
It really is important to click on "assume linear model."  For now, please take my word for it.
Cathy knows what she is talking about.
Now click on Solve.  Excel solver will obtain the optimum value for the decision variables.
That's the end for our help with this problem.  You do need to answer some more questions.  But we know you can do it without help.
Goodbye from Cathy and me until we meet again.
